title: Candidate heuristic signal buckets - Marin Alvarez (scratchpad)
content:
Quick context
- Candidate: senior infra/runtime candidate, ~7y infra/ML infra experience; last two roles were at small infra startups (gpu orchestration / autoscaling svc).
- Interview loop: phone screen (40m), system-design + runtime deep dive (90m), paired troubleshooting (60m).
- My read: strong practical heuristics, tends to default to pragmatic tradeoffs, sketches good operational runbooks. Some gaps around kernel-level perf tuning and low-level attention optimizations (quant kernels).

Signal buckets (raw impressions; for calibration later)
1) Core systems intuition (HIGH)
- Clear mental model for request routing, backpressure, and autoscaling signals. Uses concrete examples (token-per-second, queueing delay).
- Good at mapping from service-level objectives to observable metrics.
- Notes-to-self: asked for a simple sketch of a routing fallback policy and they produced a plausible policy with fast-fail thresholds.

2) Latency vs cost framing (HIGH)
- Explicitly framed choices: aggressive batching vs tail latency; advocated for dynamic batching + fast-path for <8-token requests.
- Suggests using two tiers of backends (low-latency small-batch, high-throughput large-batch) + circuit-breaker.

3) Model internals and kernels (LOW-MED)
- Knows high-level quantization benefits and memory tradeoffs. Less confident on math of int8 kernels and custom CUDA kernels.
- When pushed, deferred to existing library primitives rather than kernel micro-optimizations (not necessarily a negative given team focus).

4) Debugging under pressure (MED)
- Paired task: reproduced a flaky batch scheduling bug quickly, used logs + local tracing. Missing one edge-case where KV cache eviction interplay caused stale outputs.
- Reaction under time pressure: calm, verbalized hypotheses; could be comfortable on-call.

5) Architecture communication (MED-HIGH)
- Diagrams clear, concise. Explains tradeoffs to hypothetical PM/infra partner. Good at surfacing rollback/fallback plans.

6) Unknowns & red flags (LOW)
- Little recent hands-on with attention kernel-level profiling. If this role needs deep kernel hacking (very low-level CUDA), candidate may need ramp.
- Some short answers about long-running distributed checkpointing strategies were a bit hand-wavy. Possible gap in durable checkpoint design for PB-scale models.

Confidence tokens (subjective)
- Overall hire tilt: cautious-yes for senior IC on serving-runtime/infra.
- Recommend pairing-engagement prior to offer: 1-week paid contractor pairing to validate kernel-level debugging and checkpointing design.

Risk tiling (quick matrix)
- Ramp cost: medium (4-6 weeks to be independently productive on our kernel stack)
- Impact if wrong hire: medium-high (slows open-source model onboarding for the team for a quarter)
- Mitigation: paid pairing, targeted training, buddy-up with kernel engineer for first 8 weeks.

Open questions to resolve before final recommendation
- Exact depth of CUDA/attention-kernel exposure (ask for a code sample or walk a repo section).
- Prior ownership: which parts of their past infra repos did they own vs contributed to? (ownership matters for parallel ramps).
- Post-offer: what specific ramp plan would they propose for the first 60 days on Redwood?

Suggested follow-ups (practical)
- Quick repo read exercise: give them a small PR in our infra repo (label: "small-ops") to evaluate code style and comfort with the stack.
- Pairing task: 3x 90m sessions with one kernel engineer + one infra engineer to triage a synthetic KV cache eviction bug and design a checkpointing sketch.
- Ask them to write a 1-page playbook for live incident where model-serving fallback triggers — want to see runbook depth.

Interview snippets (verbatim paraphrases I captured)
- "I usually bias to clear observable signals — queueing time and CPU utilization — before tuning batching heuristics."
- "If the kernel path is a black box, treat it like a service: version it, have fallback quantized variants, and measure regressions at canary."

Flags to call out in panel
- Not a deep CUDA/kernel hacker, but pragmatic. Panel should weigh whether role needs that deep kernel expertise or more serving + orchestration experience.

Panel vote recommendation (my suggestion)
- Option A: Move to take-home + paid pairing (preferred).
- Option B: If team needs immediate kernel expert, pass.

Quick scoring (0-5 scale)
- Systems design: 4
- Debugging / on-call: 4
- Kernel/low-level perf: 2.5
- Communication: 4
- Ownership / shipping: 3.5

Notes-to-self before sync with hiring PM
- Share example PR for repo exercise (ENG-4823 references a small ops change).
- Loop-in Priya for kernel-pairing availability weeks 44-45.
- Draft a short contractor engagement agreement if panel greenlights paid pairing.

Bottom-line (two-sentence summary)
- Strong operational systems thinker who will land well on orchestration, routing, and observability work. Not the person to hand a CUDA kernel to and expect a micro-optimized win on day one. Consider a paid pairing step to reduce hiring risk.

Unresolved scribbles (raw)
- Could they design an autoscaler that is model-aware (seq-len distribution aware)? They sketched it (preferential routing by expected token compute) but need code evidence.
- Ask for a small tracing snippet they wrote (preferably in Go/Python) to validate instrumentation style.

End of scratchpad
